findings.title: Integer division truncates percentage before multiplying
findings.description: `pct = spent // b["limit_cents"] * 100` performs integer division first, so pct can only ever be a multiple of 100 (0, 100, 200, ...) regardless of actual spend. It should be `spent * 100 // b["limit_cents"]` (or use float division). As written, any spend below 100% of the limit always yields pct == 0, so no alert ever fires until spend fully reaches or exceeds the budget — defeating the entire purpose of an '80% warning' feature.

findings.title: Threshold comparison uses > instead of >=, and combined with truncation bug never fires near 80%
findings.description: The PR description says alerts should fire when spend 'has reached' the threshold percentage, implying pct >= threshold_pct should alert. Using `>` means spend exactly at the threshold (e.g. spent exactly 80% of limit) is not flagged. Combined with the truncation bug above, in practice alerts only fire once spend reaches/exceeds 200% of the budget, since pct only takes values 0, 100, 200, ...

findings.title: Division by zero when a budget limit is 0 or missing
findings.description: `spent // b["limit_cents"]` will raise ZeroDivisionError if a budget row has limit_cents == 0. Nothing in this diff (or visible schema) guarantees limit_cents is always positive, so a zero/misconfigured budget will crash the whole alerts call instead of being handled gracefully.

findings.title: No validation of threshold_pct argument
findings.description: threshold_pct is accepted from the caller with no bounds checking. A negative value would cause every budgeted category to alert regardless of actual spend, and values are not validated to be within a sane 0-100+ range, which could produce confusing/incorrect UI warnings if misused by a caller.

findings.title: No tests added for budget_alerts
findings.description: The diff introduces a new public function budget_alerts() with nontrivial percentage/threshold logic but adds no unit tests. Given the severity of the truncation and comparison bugs above, basic tests (e.g., spend at 50%, exactly 80%, 99%, 100%, over 100%, and zero-limit budget) would have caught these defects before merge.
